phoneme_profile.description: High central or retracted unrounded vowel; its exact realization varies by speaker, context and analysis.
phoneme_profile.phonological_status: The relationship between /i/ and /ɨ/ is debated: analyses include separate phonemes and contextually conditioned allophones.
phoneme_profile.distribution_note: In native Russian vocabulary, [ɨ] is strongly associated with non-palatalized consonant contexts; the distribution is not a simple universal rule.

historical_graphics.widely_accepted_origin: A Cyrillic ligature combining yerъ (Ъ) and i (І or И), conventionally represented as ЪІ / ЪИ.
historical_graphics.dating: The development was gradual; do not assign a single invention year without a cited manuscript witness.
historical_graphics.caution: The graphic origin of the letter does not mean that the modern vowel [ɨ] was created by mechanically combining the sounds of Ъ and І.

historical_phonology.yer_note: Old Church Slavonic ъ and ь represented reduced vowels (yers); their later outcomes depended on language, position and sound change.
historical_phonology.caution: Do not describe ъ as simply becoming modern [ɨ] in every context. The history of the vowel and the history of the grapheme are related but distinct questions.

comparative_slavic.polish_y: A related high central/centralized vowel category in Polish, but its phonetic realization and phonological pattern are not identical to Russian /ɨ/.
comparative_slavic.ukrainian_y: Ukrainian и has its own phonetic and phonological profile; it should not be treated as an exact equivalent of Russian ы.
comparative_slavic.rule: Shared Slavic transcription symbols do not establish identical pronunciation or direct letter-to-letter descent.

orthographic_history.civil_script: The Petrine civil-type reform of the early eighteenth century standardized printed letterforms; avoid claiming that one decree created the modern glyph in exactly its present shape.
orthographic_history.1917_1918_reform: The reforms changed several orthographic conventions but did not abolish the letter Ы.
orthographic_history.transliteration: Latin transliteration depends on the adopted standard and context; Y is common in some systems but is not a universal phonetic equivalence.

interpretive_layer.title: Philosophy of the hard sign and the soft echo
interpretive_layer.thesis: The image of a union between a hard-sign component and an i-component can serve as a metaphor for graphic synthesis.
interpretive_layer.numerology: The proposed sum 16 + 10 = 26 is not an established etymological or historical explanation; Ъ has no ordinary independent numeral value in the standard Cyrillic numeral system.
